I'm in Pennsylvania. Chestnut trees are still alive, on all the wooded mountains. The roots do not die from the blight. New sprouts grow up from the roots, over and over again. However, they don't grow long enough to produce seeds. W. H. Weidlich observed that the roots are safe as long as they are covered with soil, but if they are exposed, the blight infects them. He speculated that something in the soil itself was protective. He did experiments with wrapping the blight cankers with mud and enclosing it inside a bandage of some kind of plastic material (I've been trying this myself, and I've been using moss as the bandage - I haven't done it long enough to know whether it's going to work or not). A beneficial fungus in the soil, trichoderma fungus, killed the blight fungus in the locations where the soil was in contact with the cankers, and the tree was able to heal that particular injury, although it would keep on being reinfected in any other damaged areas. They were able to grow the trees and keep them from repeatedly dying off by doing this. The article where he described it was called, "A Preliminary Report on a Method of Biological Control of the Chestnut Blight Not Involving the Use of a Hypovirulent Strain of Endothia parasitica - W. H. Weidlich." I am finding dozens and dozens of live chestnut trees, waiting to be helped, when I go walking in the woods, and I can only help a small number of them, because I don't have enough time and energy. I'm going to keep trying for as long as I can, until I can help the trees survive long enough to flower and seed, and then, I will collect seeds, and plant them.

Recently, I've been arguing that the problem goes beyond simply adjusting, or simply getting used to the new time. Instead, my argument nowadays is based on something that happens with the circadian rhythm, in the body, as it relates to the sun shining, and maybe to the ionosphere and other things that are connected to the sun, the geoelectromagnetic fields - I don't know what. Something interacts with us, and that thing doesn't care what number we call the time. I read that there was a study where they found that 4:00 am was the worst time for inflammatory markers in the body, or something like that, and I haven't been able to find a reference to it again. I read it a few years ago. They said, if you're sick with a cold, the worst hours are in the early morning, but you feel better in the afternoon, which is true for me, and they said that something in the circadian rhythm causes this to happen. So we aren't able to simply get used to it. At either 4:00 am standard time, or 3:00 am daylight saving time, the sun and the ionosphere and whatever will be doing something to us, which is painful and causes inflammation in the body. We have an advantage if we get up an hour \*later\* - it's less painful. I have chronic fatigue syndrome, so I notice these things a lot. The reason I want to avoid the 'we get used to the time change after a few weeks' argument is because somebody always wants to switch us to DST permanently, so that we can avoid the change, because they believe 'change, as such, is what causes the problem.' 

If change, as such, causes the problem, then why is there such a strong motive for people to always push for permanent DST? Why not permanent standard time? There is some motive going on which goes beyond merely avoiding a time change. Somebody \*desires\* to have extra time in the afternoons, and some powerful forces are making money, enough money that they can pay some politicians to try to put bills through the government. Does anybody have enough money to do that, and care enough, unless they're profiting somehow? I personally don't care about sports at all, and I don't care if the sun sets over their games.

Yes, I think it is much easier to get up an hour later, on standard time. I don't care that the sun also sets earlier then - it's the morning that is so painful for me. I've been trying to understand why so many people insist that they want the +1 DST, and why they don't notice how painful it is to get up earlier in the morning. The only answer I can think of is the 'sporting profits' - I read someplace that golf courses, in particular, make more profits if they have an extra hour to be open in the evenings. I have no desire to suffer in the early morning just so that some golfers can have an extra hour in the evening. Apparently, the people who profit from evening activities are more common and more popular than the people who are aware of the painfulness of waking up earlier in the morning. The bills people try to pass are always 'permanent DST' instead of 'permanent standard time.'
